en: Abhidhānottara 8 = palm-leaf manuscript = Raghu Vīra’s manuscript reproduction by Lokesh Chandra
Now, there is another procedure.
Upon a delightful eight-petalled lotus, beautiful with its universal petals,
one should meditate upon the King of Lotuses in the center of a solar mandala;
its pericarp is a universal vajra with five prongs and four faces.
There, in the center of the hub, is the mark of the solar disc;
there upon its back are the vowels and consonants (ālikāli), while in the center is the line of emptiness.
Having transformed oneself through the reversal [of ordinary perception] into Vajrasattva, one becomes the supreme Heruka.

One should draw Bhairava and Kālarātri, who have five faces, twelve arms, and three eyes, and who are fierce and formidable; they stand in the *mālīḍha* posture or are situated in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, with [the goddess] trampled under their feet.
Clad in a tiger skin, overwhelmed by compassion and wrath,
adorned with a crown of skulls and a crescent moon as his crest,
his head-turban trampled by a double-vajra (viśvavajra), and imbued with the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) beginning with the erotic;
One should visualize [the deity] wearing a garland of human heads, adorned with fifty [ornaments], and embellished with a necklace, a breast-plate, earrings, and a crest-jewel;
one should likewise contemplate the six mudrās: the sacred thread and the ashes.
In his two arms embraced by Vārāhī are a skull-cup and a bell;
in the other two arms he wears the fresh hide of Mahābhairava as his garment;
and in the third right hand, he makes the gesture of a trident with a gaping vajra and a triple banner.
In the fourth [hand] he holds a five-pronged trident, in the fifth an axe,
and in the sixth a vajra and a *ḍamaru* drum.
In the third left hand is a khaṭvāṅga, in the fourth a vajra-noose,
in the fifth a curved knife, and in the sixth the head of Rudra.

In front [of him] is the Blessed Lady, embraced by Vārāhī; she is of the same color [as her consort], two-armed, one-faced, and three-eyed; her hair is adorned with a crown, she is naked, and her girdle is decorated with fragments;
her left arm embraces [the consort], and her skull-cup is filled with bodhicitta.
On the right, she threatens all directions with a threatening-knife of evil;
possessing a brilliance like the fire at the end of an aeon, she flows with blood and is fond of it.
She encircles her two shanks, she who is the supreme bliss of great happiness.
Deformed and of fierce aspect, yet overwhelmed by compassion and passion,
one should meditate upon Vajraheruka, who has Vajrasattva as his crown,
and whose faces are sky-blue, yellow, red, green, and white.
One should likewise meditate upon the Fierce, the Erotic, the Disgusting,
and the Peaceful [moods], as well as the elements, the efforts, and the aggregates, along with the assembly of attendants:
Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī.
She has four arms, one face, and three eyes; she has the form of Rudra.
Seated in the half-lotus posture, she is supreme and clad in the directions as her garment. Adorned with a crown of skulls, her hair is loose, and she shines resplendently.
The goddess Pañcamudrā, who accomplishes desire and liberation,
should be placed in the east, south, west, and north— white,
yellow, red, and green, eager for passion.
She holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a bell, a ḍamaru drum, and a flaying knife.
In the intermediate directions are four vases filled with the nectar of primordial wisdom;
a skull-cup filled with milk is placed upon a vase.
One should arrange them in a counter-clockwise direction;
having summoned the Jñānasattva, one should manifest him through worship and praise.
One should meditate upon the supreme state, which is the arrangement of mind, speech, and body.
HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ: one should visualize [the deity].
One should recite the mantra that bestows all accomplishments with the method of generation:
OṂ ŚRĪ VAJRA HE HE RU RU KAṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ ḌĀKINĪJĀLASAMVARA SVĀHĀ.
Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the heart and the near-heart mantra.
Oṃ vajravairocanī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye varṇanīye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the heart and near-heart mantra of the Goddess.
Oṃ ḍākinī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | <Oṃ lāme hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā |> Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ rūpiṇīye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
One should emanate a dense array of wrathful deities that pervade the three worlds.
Endowed with meditative cultivation, one should recite [the mantra], withdrawing [the emanations] while maintaining the nature of their radiation.
The abiding of body, speech, and mind throughout the three realms without exception—
this should be recited during the time of arising from meditation upon the two armors:
Oṃ haḥ, Vajrasattva in the heart.
*Namaḥ* is at the head, Vairocana;
*svāhā* <*hūṃ*> is at the crest-lock, Padmanarteśvara;
*vauṣaṭ* is on the two shoulders, Heruka.
HŪṂ HŪṂ HOḤ: Vajrasūrya at the eyes; PHAṬ HAṂ: Paramāśva in all the limbs;
OṂ VAṂ: Vajravārāhī at the navel.
Hāṃ yāṃ, Yāminī at the heart; Hrīṃ moṃ, Mohanī at the face;
Hreṃ hrīṃ, Sañcālanī at the head.
HŪṂ HŪṂ at the crown of the head is Saṃtrāsanī;
PHAṬ HŪṂ on all limbs is Caṇḍikā as the weapon-mantra.
Thus, through the equality of existence and non-existence, the practitioner of the yoga of mantra and form should dwell at ease in the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, concerning the sequence of the sections of the Pīṭha, from the Abhidhānottara.
